title: Number Systems — Chapter Summary
intro: This chapter walks through the family of numbers a Class 10 student needs to handle confidently: natural numbers, whole numbers, integers and rational numbers. Each new set fixes a limitation of the previous one, and rational numbers in particular have a clean decimal-expansion rule that ties prime factorisation to terminating vs recurring decimals.

sections.heading: Natural and Whole Numbers
bullets: Natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, ...} are the counting numbers.
Whole numbers W = {0, 1, 2, 3, ...} extend N by including 0.
Every natural number is a whole number, but 0 is whole and not natural.
N has a smallest element (1) but no largest; the same is true for W with smallest element 0.
Both N and W are closed under addition and multiplication, but not under subtraction or division.

sections.heading: Integers
bullets: Integers Z = {..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ...} extend W by including negative numbers.
Z is closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication.
Z is NOT closed under division: e.g. 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 ∉ Z.
On the number line, integers to the right of 0 are positive; those to the left are negative; 0 is neither.
The opposite (additive inverse) of an integer a is −a, and a + (−a) = 0.

branches.label: Addition
details: Same signs: add magnitudes, keep sign
Different signs: subtract magnitudes, sign of the larger

sections.heading: Rational Numbers
bullets: A rational number is any number of the form p/q where p, q ∈ Z and q ≠ 0.
Every integer is rational (n = n/1), but not every rational is an integer.
Equivalent rationals: p/q = (kp)/(kq) for any non-zero integer k.
Standard (lowest) form requires HCF(|p|, |q|) = 1 and a positive denominator.
Rational numbers are dense: between any two distinct rationals there are infinitely many more.

branches.label: Closure
details: a + b ∈ Q for all a, b ∈ Q

branches.label: Inverse
details: a + (−a) = 0; every rational has an additive inverse

sections.heading: Operations on Rational Numbers
bullets: To add or subtract, use a common denominator (LCM of the denominators is the most efficient choice).
Multiplication: (a/b) × (c/d) = (ac)/(bd); reduce afterwards.
Division: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c) — multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor.
Q is closed under +, −, × and division-by-nonzero.
Distributive property: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c (multiplication distributes over addition).

sections.heading: Decimal Representation
bullets: Every rational has a decimal expansion that is either terminating or non-terminating recurring.
Terminating example: 7/8 = 0.875.
Non-terminating recurring example: 1/3 = 0.333... = 0.3̄.
Conversion (recurring → fraction): set up x with a power of 10 multiplier, subtract, and solve. E.g. 0.6̄: 10x − x = 6 → x = 6/9 = 2/3.
Rule: p/q in lowest terms has a terminating decimal iff q = 2^m × 5^n; otherwise the decimal is non-terminating recurring.

key_takeaways: N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q — each extension closes a previously impossible operation.
0 is whole but not natural; negative numbers are integers but not whole.
A rational number is exactly one that can be written as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0.
Rational arithmetic (+, −, ×, ÷ by non-zero) always produces a rational.
p/q in lowest terms has a terminating decimal iff its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and 5.
Rationals are dense: there are infinitely many between any two distinct rationals.

glossary.definition: A counting number; element of N = {1, 2, 3, ...}.
A natural number or 0; element of W = {0, 1, 2, 3, ...}.
A natural number, its negative or 0; element of Z = {..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ...}.
A number expressible as p/q with p, q integers and q ≠ 0; element of Q.
A fraction p/q is in lowest terms when HCF(|p|, |q|) = 1 and q > 0.
Two rationals p/q and r/s with ps = qr; they represent the same value.
For a rational a, the number −a satisfying a + (−a) = 0.
For a non-zero rational a/b, the number b/a; their product is 1.
A set is closed under an operation if applying that operation to any two elements produces an element in the same set.
A decimal expansion that ends after finitely many digits, e.g. 0.375.
A non-terminating decimal in which a block of digits repeats forever, e.g. 0.3̄ = 0.333...
The bar drawn over the repeating block of digits in a recurring decimal.
The property that between any two distinct rational numbers there are infinitely many other rationals.
